lesson.grammar_point: self-repair and reformulation with I mean, or rather, let me rephrase that and what I meant was

listenings.text: I have worked as a conference interpreter for twenty years, and I can tell you a secret: experts make mistakes all the time when they speak. They say the wrong year, the wrong number, sometimes the wrong country. The difference between a good speaker and a nervous one is not the mistake. It is the repair. A good speaker corrects himself in two seconds and moves on. He says, sorry, I mean two thousand and nineteen, or, let me rephrase that. A nervous speaker stops, apologizes for a long time, and loses the audience. My advice: do not hide a slip of the tongue, and do not make it bigger than it is. Correct it, briefly, and continue.

During a hearing last month, a director of the agency said that the new rule would apply to all concessions. Everyone in the room started writing. Two minutes later, she stopped and said, sorry, let me qualify that. What I meant was all new concessions, not the existing ones. Or rather, the existing ones can choose to join. That correction changed everything for my clients. If she had not corrected herself, we would have spent a week preparing for the wrong scenario. Afterwards, I asked for the verbatim transcript, just to double-check. And I told my team: when an official corrects herself, the correction is usually the most important sentence of the day.
